newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Evacuation flight leaves tense Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Evacuation flight leaves tense Sierra Leone.

text.p: A Boeing 747 carrying 392 evacuees fleeing insecurity after Sunday's coup in Sierra Leone left Freetown for London on Thursday after a confrontation between Nigerian and Sierra Leonean troops contesting control of the runway.
Nigeria has sent hundreds of troops into Sierra Leone in a show of force under a regional plan to reinstate ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Sierra Leonean troops have allowed the Nigerians to continue controlling the airport, which has been under their care as part of regional accords on peacekeeping in neighbouring Liberia.
However, their relationship since the coup has been described as "correct but not cordial".

"There was a confrontation between the two sides who control opposite ends of the runway. A shot was fired as the evacuees were queueing to board the plane and everyone took defensive positions on the tarmac," a British diplomat told Reuters.
He said the shot had been fired by a Sierra Leonean soldier.

No one was hurt in the incident, which witnesses said was exacerbated by the refusal of the Sierra Leoneans to allow a Nigerian C-130 Hercules to land with troops and supplies. The Nigerians insisted on landing the plane.
U.S. Marines will evacuate about 250 U.S. citizens by helicopter to a U.S. Navy ship, the Kearsarge, on Friday and then fly them to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea.

Foreigners who took refuge in two beachside hotels to escape looting and lawlessness were flown across the wide river estuary to Lungi airport by helicopter. On Wednesday, about 400 foreigners left by plane, helicopter and boat.

"It wasn't the welcome I had hoped for," said Canadian George Cone, 42, from Calgary, who arrived only a week ago on his first trip to Africa to organise training for a cellular phone company setting up a network in Sierra Leone.
Sierra Leoneans in Washington demonstrated against the coup.

Freetown's ambassador there, John Leigh, said he wanted the 1,200 Marines aboard the Kearsarge to support the Nigerian troops "to bring in law and order" and end a "reign of terror" by the coup leaders, whom he described as "wild savages".

Trade unions and other civil groups have called on people to stay at home in protest against the coup. City centre streets were deserted apart from a few soldiers whose behaviour was in no way menacing.
An armoured car and an automatic machinegun were set up outside the bullet-pocked presidential offices at State House.
The new military authorities who seized power on Sunday blamed harassment of civilians on former servicemen and escaped prisoners in army uniform and warned they would be arrested.
The most prominent escaped prisoner is the new head of state, Major Johnny Paul Koromah.

Koromah, 33, was among those freed from Freetown's Pademba Road prison early on Sunday at the start of the coup. He was detained on treason charges over an earlier alleged coup attempt against Kabbah, who flew to Guinea on Sunday.

Koromah's Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) set up hotlines for the public to complain about harassment and looting, though it was unlikely many people would risk reporting looting that witnesses say is carried out mainly by soldiers.
"Major Johnny Paul Koromah and his comrades should consider the party over and negotiate their return to the barracks," said a commentary on Nigerian state radio.
"It will be the wisest thing to do, because ECOWAS wants the military quickly out of politics, and because Nigeria shares this resolve."
